label: Lesson 0
title: How the electromagnetic wave was discovered
summary: The wave picture of light was not handed to us ready-made. This lesson follows the chain of evidence that produced it: interference and diffraction made light a wave, polarisation proved the wave is transverse, Ørsted and Faraday joined electricity to magnetism, Maxwell's equations predicted a wave travelling at the speed of light, Hertz caught one in the laboratory, and the fall of the aether left the oscillating fields to carry the wave themselves.
source: Written fresh; history of the electromagnetic wave

intro.text: The wave picture of light was not handed to us ready-made. It was assembled slowly, over about two hundred years, by people who each answered one stubborn question. Interference and diffraction told us light is a wave; polarisation told us the wave is *transverse*; induction tied electricity to magnetism; Maxwell's equations turned that union into a prediction of a wave travelling at the speed of light; and Hertz caught the wave in the laboratory.

This lesson follows that path, because knowing *how* the picture was earned makes the picture itself easier to trust. There is no heavy mathematics here; the aim is to see why each step was needed and what forced the next one, so that when Lesson 1 states the conclusions flatly you already know where they came from.

intro.title: The conclusion, compressed
intro.body: Light is a transverse wave whose oscillations are electric and magnetic fields. Interference showed it is a wave, polarisation showed the wave is transverse, Faraday's induction showed the fields are real, and Maxwell showed the fields alone reproduce the measured speed of light.

sections.title: First, light proved to be a wave
sections.summary: Newton first pictured light as a stream of particles travelling in straight lines; interference and diffraction then showed it must be a wave, which early physicists imagined as a vibration of a material medium, the aether.
keyPoints: Before Young, the dominant picture was Newton's: light as a stream of tiny particles, or corpuscles, travelling in straight lines.
Interference and diffraction are wave effects; Young's fringes in 1801 established light as a wave.
The early wave picture assumed the vibration was in a material medium, the luminiferous aether.
Nothing yet said what the wave was made of; that was still an open question.

blocks.text: Before that, the dominant picture was Newton's. In his *Opticks* (1704) he argued that light is a stream of tiny particles, which he called *corpuscles*, thrown out by a source and travelling in straight lines. Particles explain a good deal at once: they cast sharp shadows, they bounce off a mirror to give reflection, and if they are pulled slightly toward a denser medium as they cross its surface they bend toward the normal, which is refraction.

blocks.title: Newton's corpuscles
blocks.body: Newton's light particles were not atoms in the modern sense. They were small, featureless *corpuscles* that carried the light and moved in straight lines. The picture held for a century largely because it, and Newton's great authority, explained reflection and refraction so simply.

blocks.text: By the start of the nineteenth century the particle picture of Newton was under strain. Thomas Young's two-slit experiment (1801) produced bright and dark bands where two beams of light overlapped. Adding two lights should always give more light, never darkness. Dark fringes appear only if light arrives as a wave, so that a crest from one beam can cancel a trough from the other. Diffraction, the bending of light around edges, pointed the same way.

blocks.alt: A horizontal timeline of seven milestones: Young's interference fringes in 1801, Malus's polarisation in 1808, Ørsted's current deflecting a needle in 1820, Faraday's induction in 1831, Maxwell's prediction of the speed of light in 1865, Hertz's radio waves in 1887, and Einstein's conclusion in 1905 that no medium is needed. The milestones are coloured by theme: wave nature, fields joined, and electromagnetic wave.
blocks.caption: Seven milestones in the making of the wave picture. Young and Malus established the wave and its transverse nature; Ørsted and Faraday joined electricity and magnetism; Maxwell predicted a wave at the speed of light; Hertz measured one; and Einstein showed none needs a medium. The colours group the stages.

blocks.text: So light was a wave. But a wave is a pattern in *something*, and nobody had seen what was waving. Following the physics of the day, everyone assumed a material medium that filled all of space — the *luminiferous aether* — just as sound waves need air. That assumption would survive for most of a century before it fell.

blocks.title: A wave in what?
blocks.body: Interference proved light has wave behaviour, but it could not say what is oscillating. The answer, fields rather than matter, had to wait for the joining of electricity and magnetism.

sections.title: Longitudinal and transverse waves, and polarisation
sections.summary: A wave may vibrate along its direction of travel (longitudinal) or at right angles to it (transverse). Only a transverse wave can be polarised, and that light can be forced into a single plane is direct evidence that its oscillations travel across, not along, the beam.
keyPoints: A longitudinal wave vibrates along its direction of travel and shows compressions and rarefactions; sound in air is the example.
A transverse wave vibrates at right angles to its travel and shows crests and troughs; light and a wave on a rope are examples.
Polarisation restricts a transverse wave to a single plane of vibration; a polarising filter transmits only the component along its axis.
Only a transverse wave can be polarised, because only it has a plane of oscillation to select; crossed filters at 90° block the light.
Malus found polarised light by reflection in 1808; Fresnel and Arago showed in 1819 that beams polarised at right angles do not interfere.
That light can be polarised proved the light wave is transverse.

blocks.text: A wave can oscillate in two ways with respect to its travel. In a *longitudinal* wave the medium vibrates back and forth *along* the direction of travel; sound in air is the everyday example, and the pattern you see is compressions where the air crowds together and rarefactions where it spreads apart. In a *transverse* wave the vibration is *at right angles* to the direction of travel, like a wave on a rope that you shake up and down; the pattern is crests above the axis and troughs below it.

blocks.alt: A longitudinal wave drawn as a row of particles that bunch together at compressions and spread apart at rarefactions, with a highlighted particle vibrating back and forth along the direction of travel.
blocks.caption: A longitudinal wave. The particles move back and forth *along* the direction of travel, so the wave shows compressions and rarefactions rather than crests and troughs. The highlighted particle's vibration lies on the travel axis.

blocks.alt: A transverse wave drawn as a sine curve with crests above the equilibrium line and troughs below it, and a highlighted particle vibrating up and down at right angles to the direction of travel.
blocks.caption: A transverse wave. The particles move *at right angles* to the direction of travel, giving crests and troughs. Because the vibration lies in a plane across the beam, this is the type of wave that can be polarised.

head: Property
Longitudinal
Transverse
rows: at right angles to the direction of travel
sound in air, a compression wave in a spring
light, a wave on a rope or on water

blocks.title: Polarisation, plainly
blocks.body: To *polarise* a wave is to restrict its vibration to a single plane. A polarising filter lets through only the part of the vibration along its transmission axis. This is possible only for a transverse wave, whose vibration already lies at right angles to the beam, so it has a plane to choose. A longitudinal wave vibrates along the beam, so there is nothing to restrict.

blocks.alt: Unpolarised light with vibrations in many directions passing through a polarising filter, which lets through only the component in a single plane, giving vertically polarised light.
blocks.caption: A polarising filter selects one plane of vibration out of many. Only a transverse wave offers a plane to select, which is why polarisation is the fingerprint of a transverse wave.

blocks.alt: Unpolarised light passes a first filter to become vertically polarised, then meets a second filter whose axis is horizontal, which transmits nothing.
blocks.caption: Crossed polarisers. The first filter leaves light vibrating in one plane; a second filter at right angles to the first then removes it completely. A longitudinal wave could never show this, and the effect is the basis of glare-reducing sunglasses.

blocks.text: The evidence arrived in two parts. In 1808 Étienne-Louis Malus noticed that light reflected from a glass surface was polarised. A few years later, in 1819, Augustin-Jean Fresnel and François Arago found that two beams polarised at right angles refuse to interfere: they simply add as light. That is impossible for a longitudinal wave, where every beam would share the same axis of vibration.

blocks.title: The idea in one line
blocks.body: Polarisation is a property only a transverse wave can have, so the observation that light can be polarised proves its oscillations are perpendicular to the direction it travels.

sections.title: Electricity and magnetism were joined
sections.summary: Ørsted showed that a current deflects a compass needle and Faraday showed that a changing magnetic field creates an electric field, revealing that fields carry energy and act on matter.
keyPoints: Ørsted (1820) found that an electric current deflects a nearby compass needle, linking electricity and magnetism.
Faraday (1831) found that a changing magnetic field creates an electric field, and a changing electric field creates a magnetic field.
This showed that fields are physical things that carry energy, not merely a way of drawing forces.
The mutual creation of one field by a change in the other is exactly what later lets a wave sustain itself.

blocks.text: While the debate about the wave nature of light continued, a separate discovery was unfolding. In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a wire carrying a current made a nearby compass needle swing. Electricity and magnetism, treated as separate subjects for centuries, were connected.

Michael Faraday pushed the connection further. In 1831 he found that a *changing* magnetic field produces an electric field, and a changing electric field produces a magnetic field — the effect behind every generator and transformer. Crucially, these fields do real work: they carry energy and exert forces.

blocks.title: Fields are not bookkeeping
blocks.body: It is tempting to treat a field as a clever way of describing forces at a distance. Faraday's experiments show otherwise: a field stores energy and can push on charge, so it behaves like a physical thing in its own right.

blocks.text: Keep this mutual creation in mind. A changing electric field gives rise to a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field gives rise to an electric field. That single fact is what, in the next section, allows a disturbance to keep regenerating itself as it travels.

blocks.title: Why this matters for light
blocks.body: Because each field can create the other, a pair of oscillating fields can travel through empty space without any material to support it. The seed of the electromagnetic wave is already here.

sections.title: Maxwell predicted an electromagnetic wave
sections.summary: Combining the known laws of electricity and magnetism, Maxwell derived a wave equation, found its speed to be 1 over the square root of ε₀μ₀ — the measured speed of light — and predicted that light is an electromagnetic wave.
keyPoints: Maxwell (1861-1865) gathered the laws of electricity and magnetism into four equations.
In empty space they combine into a wave equation, so a self-sustaining electromagnetic wave should exist.
Its predicted speed is c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀), which comes out to about 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the speed of light.
The equations also force E, B and the direction of travel to be mutually perpendicular: the wave is transverse.

blocks.text: James Clerk Maxwell set about writing the known laws of electricity and magnetism as a small set of equations. When he combined them for empty space, something unexpected fell out. A changing electric field creates a magnetic field; a changing magnetic field creates an electric field; so a disturbance can renew itself and march forward. The equations took the form of a *wave equation*.

blocks.caption: Maxwell's equations in empty space give a wave equation for the fields

blocks.text: The speed of that wave was fixed by two constants already measured in the laboratory: the permittivity ε₀, which measures how readily a vacuum hosts an electric field, and the permeability μ₀, the same idea for a magnetic field. The equations gave the speed as a simple combination of the two.

blocks.caption: Maxwell's predicted speed for electromagnetic waves

blocks.text: Putting in the measured numbers gave about 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. That is the measured speed of light. Maxwell drew the inescapable conclusion: light *is* an electromagnetic wave. Optics became a branch of electromagnetism, and the wave that had puzzled Young now had a definite substance, the fields themselves.

blocks.alt: An electromagnetic wave, with the electric field E oscillating vertically and the magnetic field B oscillating from side to side at right angles, both perpendicular to the direction of travel, which is marked by an arrow labelled at the speed of light c.
blocks.caption: The wave Maxwell's equations demand: **E** and **B** at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, moving forward at **c**. The transverse geometry is not a choice; it is forced by the field equations.

blocks.title: A prediction, not an observation
blocks.body: Maxwell did not observe an electromagnetic wave; no one had yet made one. He computed that if the laws of electricity and magnetism are right, such waves must exist and must travel at the speed of light. That is one of the boldest predictions in physics.

sections.title: Hertz caught the wave
sections.summary: In 1887 Hertz generated and detected electromagnetic waves in the laboratory, showing they travel at the speed of light and can be reflected, refracted and polarised like light.
keyPoints: Hertz built a spark-gap transmitter and a detector and produced radio-frequency electromagnetic waves.
The waves travelled at the speed of light and could be reflected, refracted, focused and polarised.
This confirmed we are dealing with electromagnetic waves, and that light is one: radio and light are the same phenomenon.
Radio waves and light differ only in wavelength and frequency, exactly the picture Lesson 1 states.

blocks.text: The prediction had to be tested. Between 1885 and 1889 Heinrich Hertz built an apparatus in which a spark jumping across one gap produced a burst of radiation, and a small spark across a second gap detected it. He was generating and receiving *radio* waves: electromagnetic waves at a much longer wavelength than light.

The waves behaved exactly as predicted. They travelled at the speed of light. They could be reflected by a metal sheet and brought to a focus by a curved reflector, showing they carry energy in beams. And, decisively, they could be polarised — a transverse electromagnetic wave, made and controlled in the laboratory.

blocks.title: One phenomenon, two names
blocks.body: Hertz's radio waves and visible light are the same kind of wave, differing only in wavelength and frequency. Maxwell's theory had already said so; the experiment made it plain.

blocks.text: With Hertz, the wave picture was no longer an inference about light alone. Electromagnetic waves were real, controllable objects, and their measured speed matched Maxwell's prediction to within the accuracy of the day.

sections.title: The aether fell, the fields remained
sections.summary: Michelson and Morley found no aether wind, and Einstein's relativity showed none is needed: the oscillating fields propagate themselves. What oscillates is not a material but a pair of fields.
keyPoints: The Michelson-Morley experiment (1887) found no motion of the Earth relative to any aether.
Einstein (1905) discarded the aether: electromagnetic waves need no medium.
A changing E makes a B and a changing B makes an E, so the fields sustain one another through empty space.
The final answer to 'what is waving?' is the fields themselves.

blocks.text: One problem remained. A wave was thought to need a medium, and the aether had never been detected. In 1887, the same year as Hertz's work, Albert Michelson and Edward Morley measured the speed of light in different directions as the Earth moved through space. If an aether existed, that speed should change slightly with direction. It did not. No aether wind was ever found.

In 1905 Albert Einstein removed the difficulty at the root. He discarded the aether altogether, and his theory of relativity showed that light travels through empty space without any medium at all. The medium was never there to find.

Then what is waving? The answer is the fields. A changing electric field creates a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field creates an electric field, so the two regenerate each other and a disturbance travels through the vacuum on its own. There is no material carrying it; the fields are the wave.

blocks.title: The answer to 'what oscillates?'
blocks.body: Not a material, and not space waving like a jelly, but a pair of fields, E and B, each sustaining the other as the pattern moves forward at c. That is the sentence Lesson 1 opens with, and now you know how it was earned.

cta.title: Check what you have learned
cta.body: Take the Lesson 0 quiz on how the electromagnetic wave was discovered, from interference and polarisation to Maxwell, Hertz and the fall of the aether.
cta.secondaryLabel: Next: the nature of electromagnetic radiation

questions.question: Which experiment first made a convincing case that light behaves as a wave?
questions.explanation: Young's two-slit experiment (1801) produced bright and dark fringes. Dark bands where two beams overlap can only appear if light is a wave, so that a crest of one beam cancels a trough of the other.

questions.question: Interference and diffraction are effects that a stream of particles cannot produce.
questions.explanation: Both are wave effects. Two streams of particles would simply add to give more light, never the dark fringes of destructive interference, and particles would not spread out around an edge as diffraction requires.

questions.question: Interference had established that light is a wave, yet important questions were still open. Which of these were still unknown at that stage? Select all that apply.
options: whether the waves needed a material medium
that light is a wave at all
questions.explanation: The wave nature itself was settled by interference. What remained open was what was oscillating and whether a medium (the aether) was required. Polarisation was discovered later, and it was the clue to the first open question.

questions.question: A sound wave in air cannot be polarised because it is longitudinal. What does that tell you about light, which can be polarised?
options: light's oscillations are perpendicular to its direction of travel
light must need a material medium
light is really a stream of particles
questions.explanation: Only a transverse wave has a plane of oscillation to select, so polarisation is possible only for a transverse wave. Since light can be polarised, its vibrations are transverse, at right angles to the direction of travel.

questions.question: Only a transverse wave can be polarised.
questions.explanation: A longitudinal wave vibrates along its direction of travel, so there is no sideways plane to restrict it to. Polarisation selects one plane of vibration, which only a transverse wave possesses.

questions.question: Fresnel and Arago found that two beams polarised at right angles do not interfere. Why was this result important?
options: it proved the light wave is transverse
it proved light travels at the speed of light
it proved light is made of photons
it showed that light needs no medium
questions.explanation: If the beams refused to interfere, their vibrations were in perpendicular planes. A longitudinal wave has only one axis of vibration, so it could never show this behaviour. The observation proved the light wave is transverse.

questions.question: What did Faraday's induction experiments show about fields?
options: that fields can carry energy and exert forces, so they are physical things
that fields are only a convenient way of drawing forces at a distance
that fields travel faster than light
that fields need a material medium to exist
questions.explanation: A changing magnetic field produces an electric field and vice versa, and these fields do real work: they store energy and drive currents. So they are not just bookkeeping for forces; they behave like physical things in their own right.

questions.question: A changing magnetic field can create an electric field, and a changing electric field can create a magnetic field.
questions.explanation: This mutual creation is the essence of Faraday's induction. It is also the reason an electromagnetic wave can sustain itself through a vacuum: each field keeps regenerating the other.

questions.question: Maxwell's equations predicted an electromagnetic wave travelling at a speed given by 1/√(ε₀μ₀). Why was this so striking?
options: because the value came out equal to the measured speed of light
because it came out equal to the speed of sound
because it was zero in a vacuum
because it varied with the colour of the light
questions.explanation: Two constants measured in purely electrical and magnetic experiments gave a speed of about 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the speed of light. That coincidence forced the conclusion that light is an electromagnetic wave.

questions.question: Maxwell's predicted wave speed is c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀). Using ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m and μ₀ = 1.257 × 10⁻⁶ H/m, calculate c in m/s.
What did Hertz achieve in 1887?
options: he generated and detected electromagnetic waves in the laboratory
he was the first to measure the speed of light
he proved that light needs an aether
questions.explanation: Hertz used a spark-gap transmitter and a spark detector to produce and receive radio waves. He showed they travel at the speed of light and can be reflected, refracted and polarised, confirming Maxwell's prediction.

questions.question: Which properties did Hertz's radio waves share with visible light? Select all that apply.
options: they travel at the speed of light
they can be reflected and refracted
questions.explanation: Hertz showed his waves travelled at the speed of light, could be reflected and focused, and could be polarised, all like light. They do carry energy, so the last option is false.

questions.question: What did the Michelson-Morley experiment find?
options: no motion of the Earth relative to any aether
that the speed of light depends on direction
that light is a stream of particles
that the aether is a rigid solid
questions.explanation: Michelson and Morley looked for a change in the speed of light as the Earth moved through the supposed aether. They found none, so there was no aether wind and no evidence for an aether at all.

questions.question: Electromagnetic waves need a material medium to travel through.
questions.explanation: They need no medium. After the aether was disproved, it became clear that the oscillating fields sustain each other, so the wave carries itself through a vacuum. That is how sunlight crosses empty space to reach us.

questions.question: Which observations did Newton's corpuscular (particle) theory of light explain simply?
questions.explanation: Particles travel in straight lines and can bounce (reflection) or be pulled into a denser medium (refraction), so these followed naturally. Interference, diffraction and polarisation did not.

questions.question: Which observation is most directly incompatible with light being a stream of particles?
options: dark interference fringes where two beams overlap
questions.explanation: Particles can only add up, so two overlapping beams should always give more light. Waves can cancel to give darkness, which is what the dark fringes show.

questions.question: In an interference pattern, a dark fringe appears where two waves meet because:
options: a crest of one wave cancels a trough of the other
one beam is blocked by the other
the light is absorbed by the screen
questions.explanation: Darkness is destructive interference: the two waves arrive out of step, so their displacements add to zero at that point.

questions.question: Diffraction is best described as:
options: the spreading of a wave after it passes an edge or a narrow slit
the bouncing of light from a surface
a change of colour inside a medium
the bending of a particle path by gravity
questions.explanation: A wave spreads out when part of its front is blocked. A stream of particles travelling in straight lines would not do this.

questions.question: Under Newton's particle picture, the edge of a shadow cast by an object should be:
options: ringed with bright and dark bands
questions.explanation: Particles travel in straight lines, so the shadow should have a clean edge. In practice the edge is slightly blurred and fringed, which the wave picture explains as diffraction.

questions.question: Interference requires the two overlapping waves to have a definite phase relationship.
questions.explanation: The bright and dark pattern comes from the phase difference between the waves. Without a fixed phase relationship the fringes would wash out.

questions.question: Two overlapping beams of particles can produce dark fringes.
questions.explanation: Particles simply add to the number arriving, giving more light everywhere the beams overlap. Darkness requires cancellation, which only waves can do.

questions.question: Diffraction becomes more noticeable when the size of the opening is comparable to the wavelength.
questions.explanation: When the slit width is of the same order as the wavelength, the wave spreads strongly. If the opening is far larger than the wavelength, the spreading is small and the straight-line picture nearly works.

questions.question: Which behaviours did Newton's particle theory of light explain well? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Particles travelling in straight lines account for shadows, reflection and refraction. They cannot produce stable interference fringes, which require waves.

questions.question: Which observations support the wave picture of light over the particle picture? Select all that apply.
options: diffraction of light around an edge
questions.explanation: Interference and diffraction are wave effects. Sharp shadows and reflection are explained equally well by particles, so they do not decide between the two pictures.

questions.question: For light of wavelength 600 nm, what is the smallest path difference, in nm, that produces a dark fringe in an interference pattern?
questions.explanation: A dark fringe occurs when the path difference is an odd number of half-wavelengths. The smallest nonzero value is one half-wavelength: 600/2 = 300 nm.

questions.question: Two waves arrive with a path difference of 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ m. Light of wavelength 500 nm is used. How many whole wavelengths is this path difference?
questions.explanation: Convert: 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ m = 1500 nm. Then 1500/500 = 3 whole wavelengths.

questions.question: Polarising a light wave restricts its oscillations to:
questions.explanation: A polariser passes only the component of the vibration lying in one plane, so the transmitted light oscillates in that plane alone.

questions.question: Why can a sound wave in air not be polarised?
options: its vibrations are along the direction of travel
it is inaudible at high frequency
questions.explanation: Sound in air is longitudinal: the air moves back and forth along the travel direction. There is no sideways plane to select, so polarisation is impossible.

questions.question: The fact that light can be polarised shows that light is:
questions.explanation: Only a transverse wave has a plane of vibration to select, so a wave that can be polarised must be transverse.

questions.question: In a transverse wave, the oscillation is directed:
options: perpendicular to the direction of travel
parallel to the direction of travel
opposite to the direction of travel
along the direction of energy flow
questions.explanation: By definition the displacement in a transverse wave is at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels.

questions.question: Two beams of light polarised at right angles are brought together. The result is that they:
options: do not form an interference pattern
questions.explanation: Beams whose vibrations are in perpendicular planes cannot interfere, because they never oppose each other crest-to-trough. They simply add as light.

questions.question: In a longitudinal wave the oscillation is parallel to the direction of travel.
questions.explanation: That is the defining feature of a longitudinal wave, such as sound in air, where the air moves back and forth along the wave's direction.

questions.question: A transverse wave can be polarised, but a longitudinal wave cannot.
questions.explanation: Polarisation selects a plane of vibration perpendicular to the travel direction, which only a transverse wave possesses.

questions.question: Passing light through a polarising filter changes its speed in a vacuum.
questions.explanation: The speed in a vacuum is c for all electromagnetic radiation. A polariser selects a plane of vibration but does not change the speed in vacuum.

questions.question: Which of the following are transverse waves? Select all that apply.
options: a wave on a plucked rope
a wave on the surface of water
questions.explanation: A rope wave, light and a water surface wave all oscillate at right angles to their travel direction. Sound in air is longitudinal.

questions.question: Which of the following are longitudinal waves? Select all that apply.
options: a compression wave in a spring
a wave on a stretched string
questions.explanation: Sound and a spring compression wave move along the direction of travel. Light and a string wave are transverse.

questions.question: In a transverse wave, at what angle (in degrees) is the vibration to the direction of travel?
questions.explanation: Transverse means the displacement is at right angles to the direction of travel, that is, 90°.

questions.question: A transverse wave travels 12 m along a rope in 4.0 s. What is its speed in m/s?
questions.explanation: Speed = distance / time = 12 / 4.0 = 3.0 m/s.

questions.question: A changing magnetic field produces:
questions.explanation: This is Faraday's law of induction: a changing magnetic field drives an electric field (and hence a current in a conductor).

questions.question: A changing electric field produces:
questions.explanation: The reverse of induction: a changing electric field gives rise to a magnetic field. Maxwell added this to make the picture symmetric.

questions.question: Faraday's law of induction is the principle behind the operation of:
questions.explanation: Both generators and transformers work by changing the magnetic flux through a coil, which induces an EMF.

questions.question: Ørsted's experiment showed that an electric current:
options: reduces the resistance of a wire
questions.explanation: A current-carrying wire twists a compass needle, which shows that electricity and magnetism are connected.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to call a field merely a way of 'bookkeeping' forces?
options: a field stores energy and can exert a force
a field travels faster than light
a field has no physical effects
questions.explanation: A field carries energy and pushes on charges, so it behaves like a physical entity in its own right, not just a convenient drawing.

questions.question: The mutual creation of electric and magnetic fields is important because it allows:
options: a magnet to lose its field
a current to flow without a circuit
questions.explanation: Because each changing field creates the other, a disturbance in the fields can keep regenerating itself as it travels through space.

questions.question: To create the other kind of field, a field must be changing.
questions.explanation: A steady field does not create the other kind. It is the change (the rate of change) that produces the induced field, as in induction.

questions.question: Electricity and magnetism are two entirely unrelated phenomena.
questions.explanation: Ørsted and Faraday showed they are two faces of one phenomenon: electric currents create magnetic fields and changing magnetic fields create electric fields.

questions.question: A field can exert a force on a charge placed in it.
questions.explanation: An electric field exerts a force on a charge, and a magnetic field exerts a force on a moving charge. Fields are not merely descriptive.

questions.question: Which devices rely on electromagnetic induction? Select all that apply.
options: a bar magnet lying at rest
questions.explanation: Transformers, generators and motors all involve changing magnetic flux and induced EMFs. A stationary magnet with no change produces no induction.

questions.question: Which statements about fields are correct? Select all that apply.
options: a field can exert a force on a charge
a field needs a material medium to exist
a field can be created by a changing field of the other kind
questions.explanation: Fields store energy, act on charges, and can be produced by a changing field of the other kind. They do not need a material medium.

questions.question: A coil has 200 turns. The magnetic flux through it changes by 0.010 Wb in 0.050 s. Using EMF = N ΔΦ/Δt, find the magnitude of the induced EMF in volts.
A charge of 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ C sits in an electric field of 2000 N/C. What is the force on it, in newtons?
Maxwell's equations, applied to empty space, predict:
questions.explanation: The equations combine into a wave equation, so a disturbance of the fields must travel through empty space.

questions.question: Maxwell's predicted speed for electromagnetic waves is:
questions.explanation: The speed is the inverse square root of the product of the two vacuum constants, giving about 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

questions.question: That 1/√(ε₀μ₀) equals the measured speed of light showed that:
options: light is a stream of particles
questions.explanation: The identity of the two speeds tied optics to electromagnetism and identified light as an electromagnetic wave.

questions.question: In an electromagnetic wave in vacuum, E and B are:
options: mutually perpendicular and both perpendicular to the travel direction
parallel to each other and along the travel direction
parallel to each other, both perpendicular to travel
questions.explanation: The fields are mutually perpendicular and transverse: each is at right angles to the other and to the direction of travel.

questions.question: Which constant measures how readily a vacuum hosts an electric field?
questions.explanation: The permittivity ε₀ describes the electric response of a vacuum; the permeability μ₀ describes the magnetic response.

questions.question: In a vacuum, the electric field of a plane electromagnetic wave has:
options: no component along the direction of travel
a large component along the direction of travel
a component only along the magnetic field
questions.explanation: Because ∇·E = 0 in empty space, a plane wave has no longitudinal component of E; the field is purely transverse.

questions.question: Maxwell predicted electromagnetic waves before anyone had produced one.
questions.explanation: He derived them mathematically from the field equations. Hertz produced and detected them experimentally some twenty years later.

questions.question: The speed of an electromagnetic wave in a vacuum depends on its frequency.
questions.explanation: In a vacuum all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed c, whatever their frequency or wavelength.

questions.question: In a vacuum, the electromagnetic wave is transverse.
questions.explanation: The field equations require E and B to be perpendicular to the direction of travel, so the wave is strictly transverse.

questions.question: Which of the following follow from Maxwell's equations in empty space? Select all that apply.
options: a wave equation for the fields
the need for a material medium
questions.explanation: The equations give a wave equation, a speed set by the vacuum constants, and transverse fields. They require no medium.

questions.question: Which are properties of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: It travels at c, has mutually perpendicular transverse fields, and needs no medium.

questions.question: Given c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and μ₀ = 1.257 × 10⁻⁶ H/m, find ε₀ from c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀). Give the answer in F/m.
An electromagnetic wave has an electric-field amplitude of 300 V/m. Using E/B = c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, find the magnetic-field amplitude in tesla.
Hertz's spark-gap apparatus generated and detected:
questions.explanation: A spark transmitter produced bursts of radio-frequency electromagnetic radiation, picked up by a small spark at the detector.

questions.question: Hertz showed his waves could be polarised, which demonstrated that they are:
questions.explanation: Only a transverse wave can be polarised, so this proved the waves were transverse like light.

questions.question: Hertz measured his waves to travel at:
questions.explanation: The waves travelled at c, matching Maxwell's prediction and confirming they were electromagnetic.

questions.question: Radio waves and visible light differ in:
questions.explanation: They are the same kind of wave; only wavelength and frequency differ. Their speed in vacuum and their polarisability are the same.

questions.question: Hertz focused his waves onto the detector with a curved metal reflector, showing that the waves:
options: can be reflected and carry energy in a beam
questions.explanation: Reflection and focusing show the radiation behaves like light and carries energy in a directed beam.

questions.question: The spark-gap detector responded because the arriving wave:
options: drove a spark across the gap with its oscillating field
heated the gap to melting point
questions.explanation: The oscillating electric field of the incoming wave produced a large enough field at the gap to spark across it.

questions.question: Radio waves and light are the same kind of wave, differing only in wavelength and frequency.
questions.explanation: Both are electromagnetic waves. Their place on the spectrum is set by wavelength and frequency alone.

questions.question: In a vacuum, radio waves travel more slowly than visible light.
questions.explanation: In a vacuum every electromagnetic wave travels at c. Only in a medium can different frequencies travel at slightly different speeds.

questions.question: Electromagnetic waves can be polarised because they are transverse.
questions.explanation: Polarisation selects a plane of vibration. Because the fields oscillate at right angles to travel, such a plane exists.

questions.question: Which properties did Hertz demonstrate for his waves? Select all that apply.
options: they travel at the speed of light
questions.explanation: Hertz measured the speed, reflected and focused the waves, and polarised them. They do not need air; they travel through vacuum.

questions.question: Which are true of both radio waves and visible light? Select all that apply.
options: they travel at c in vacuum
questions.explanation: Both are transverse electromagnetic waves travelling at c in vacuum and polarisable. Neither is longitudinal.

questions.question: A radio wave has a frequency of 3.0 × 10⁸ Hz. Find its wavelength in metres. Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
An FM radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz. What is its wavelength in metres? Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
Michelson and Morley set out to detect:
options: the Earth's motion through the aether
questions.explanation: They tried to measure a change in the speed of light as the Earth moved through the supposed aether.

questions.question: Their result was that the speed of light:
questions.explanation: No difference with direction was found, so there was no aether wind and no evidence for an aether.

questions.question: What sustains an electromagnetic wave through a vacuum?
questions.explanation: A changing E creates a B and a changing B creates an E, so the fields keep the wave going with no medium.

questions.question: Because a changing E makes a B and a changing B makes an E, the wave:
options: loses its fields after a metre
questions.explanation: Each part of the wave creates the next, so the disturbance propagates indefinitely through empty space.

questions.question: Einstein's theory of relativity removed the need for:
questions.explanation: Relativity described light travelling through empty space with no medium, so the aether was unnecessary.

questions.question: In an electromagnetic wave, the energy is carried by:
questions.explanation: The fields themselves carry the energy of the wave; there is no material doing the carrying.

questions.question: The speed of light in vacuum is the same in all directions.
questions.explanation: Michelson and Morley found no directional dependence, which is why no aether wind was detected.

questions.question: Sunlight can reach the Earth through the vacuum of space.
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic waves need no medium, so light crosses empty space from the Sun to the Earth.

questions.question: An electromagnetic wave can travel through a vacuum.
questions.explanation: The fields sustain each other, so no material medium is required. This is why starlight reaches us across space.

questions.question: Which were reasons the aether was abandoned? Select all that apply.
options: the aether was measured to be very dense
questions.explanation: The missing aether wind, the vacuum propagation of light, and relativity all removed the need for the aether. It was never measured to be dense.

questions.question: Which are true of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: It carries energy, needs no medium, and its fields sustain each other. It is transverse, not longitudinal.

questions.question: Light travels from the Sun, 1.5 × 10¹¹ m away, through vacuum. How long does it take to reach the Earth, in seconds? Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
A light year is the distance light travels in one year. Using c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and 1 year = 3.15 × 10⁷ s, find one light year in metres (give the coefficient, e.g. 9.5e15).
